paragraphs.text: Yi Ji is [first grade](yi-ji:definition). Anhua's raw leaf is sorted by how tender it was when picked, and Yi Ji holds the youngest leaf of the numbered lots. A grade describes the leaf that went in. It does not say which hill the leaf grew on or [how well the tea was made](yi-ji:grade-and-quality). Like every Anhua tea, this one began as [dark raw tea](anhua-dark:making): large local leaf fixed, rolled, piled, rolled again and dried. The piling is where the leaf changes in warmth and moisture, and that change is what makes it a [dark tea](dark:definition).

The leaf comes from [Anhua](anhua:where-it-is), a mountain county on the middle Zi river in north-central Hunan, at the northern foot of the Xuefeng mountains. Rice is hard to grow there, but tea does well. The county is the home of [Anhua dark tea](anhua-dark:definition), a protected origin. The warm, wet air that grows the leaf is the same air it is [piled and aged in](anhua:why-people-value-it), so the trade ties the finished tea to the place as well as to the method.

Made in 2020, the tea is six years old. Anhua tea is [kept for years](anhua-dark:ageing), and no agreed count of years marks it as aged, so this is a young tea that is still changing. Clean, dry and aired storage is what lets that change go on.

brewing.text: In a small pot or gaiwan, use water at the boil and start with a steep of about 15 to 30 seconds, a little longer each round. Pressed and aged Anhua tea is also commonly simmered in a pot.

notice.text: Pine smoke or pine resin above all, a sweet taste and aftertaste, and a mellow, thick, smooth cup; a liquor from yellow and orange to orange-red. Young tea is often smokier in the first infusions and a little bitter, sweetening as the infusions go on.

unsupported.why: The claim only tells the reader to keep the tea clean, dry and aired, away from mould and other smells. It never says that this storage is what allows the tea to keep changing, so this is a general statement no claim makes.
